1.pericope_label: I will stand upon my watch, and set me upon the tower, and will watch to see what he will say unto me, and what I shall answer when I am reproved.

schools.summary: Place the verses as the introduction to God's answer, correct the received rendering to what he will say in me, and refer the answer to the prophet's own complaint rather than to objectors.
Make the speaker the whole Church rather than a private man, and read the watchtower as patience arising from hope.
Give the chapter's argument and take the reproof as a summons to account for the mysteriousness of providence.
Reads the tower as prudence and the standing as constancy, and equips the prophet to answer the exceptions of others.

positions.position: Patience arising from hope, and more exactly the recess of the mind into which we withdraw from the world; not the prophetic office.
Prudence: the use of every help within reach, getting above the world, studying, consulting experience and continuing in prayer.
An ordinary figure drawn from climbing a height for a wide view, not to be pressed into biography.

debates.question: To whom is the answer returned?

positions.position: To objectors: the prophet is called to give account of providence, to satisfy doubters or silence quarrellers.
To his own complaint, not to any opponent.

outliers.claim: Notes that Balaam the heathen soothsayer did literally betake himself to a solitary height, but holds that a soothsayer's conduct throws no light on the customs of the Jewish prophets.
Settles only the question of the speaker, that the words are the prophet's own, and cites the Targum as introducing them that way.

themes: I will stand upon my watch, and set me upon the tower, and will watch to see what he will say unto me, and what I shall answer when I am reproved.

2.pericope_label: And the Lord answered me, and said, Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables, that he may run that readeth it. For the vision is yet for an appointed time, but at the end it shall speak, and not lie: though it tarry, wait for it; because it will surely come, it will not tarry.

schools.summary: Mark the point where the prophecy proper begins, render the running clause of a reader's eye, and object that saying the vision will not tarry contradicts what has just been said.
Take the answer as a pledge to the whole Church, require large letters so a passer-by may read at a glance, and make the delay a trial of patience.
Describe the ancient custom of publishing on tables hung in public, and deny that the clause means a careless reader can catch the sense.

debates.question: Does the clause mean a reader running by can take in the writing?

positions.position: Yes: the letters were to be large, so that anyone passing quickly might see at a glance, the writing not causing readers to stop.
It means the reader may run his eye quickly through the inscription.
No: that reading is very foolish, since God never intends his words to be understood by the careless; it means the attentive reader may speed away and save his life.

outliers.claim: Attacks the popular saying that God's book is so plain that he who runs may read, insisting no trifler understands Scripture, and jokes that if a play-bill were read as many read the Bible its readers would know as much of the one as of the other.
Calls the rendering it will not tarry unfortunate, since the prophet has just said the vision will tarry, and prefers that it shall not be behindhand on its appointed day.

themes: And the Lord answered me, and said, Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables, that he may run that readeth it.
For the vision is yet for an appointed time, but at the end it shall speak, and not lie: though it tarry, wait for it; because it will surely come, it will not tarry.

4.pericope_label: Behold, his soul which is lifted up is not upright in him: but the just shall live by his faith.

schools.summary: Reads the puffed-up soul as self-dependence that ousts God, and warns the student against importing the doctrine of justification by faith into the second clause.
Make the proud man his own executioner for want of tranquillity, and set faith against every other defence men rely on.
Keep the historical sense first, the believer escaping the siege, and treat the later apostolic use as an accommodation.

debates.question: How is the promise that the just shall live by his faith to be taken?

positions.position: Not doctrinally: the renderings righteous-by-faith and justified-by-faith cannot stand, and here the words carry no doctrinal significance, though their ethical weight is undeniable.
Historically first: the man who believed the warning escaped and saved his life, the later use being an accommodation.
Faith set against every defence by which men blind themselves, so that he who is stripped of all protections lives by seeking in God alone.
The humble man persuaded of the truth of the promises, supporting himself by a firm expectation of deliverance.

outliers.claim: Reads the two clauses as two sorts of men differently affected toward the Messiah, identifying the proud with the Scribes and Pharisees whose hearts he compares to bubbles blown up and full of wind.

Chooses among readings of the first clause, preferring that where there is elation of mind there is no tranquillity, so that the proud are their own executioners, never finding a quiet haven because some new suspicion always disturbs them.

themes: Behold, his soul which is lifted up is not upright in him: but the just shall live by his faith.

5.pericope_label: Yea also, because he transgresseth by wine, he is a proud man, neither keepeth at home, who enlargeth his desire as hell, and is as death, and cannot be satisfied, but gathereth unto him all nations, and heapeth unto him all people:

schools.summary: Settle the force of the opening particle against rival glosses and add the charges of drunkenness and insatiable greed to the arrogance already laid.
Widen the sentence past the king to the whole empire, or else refuse the Chaldean reference altogether in favour of the enemies of Christ.
Names the king, reports rival renderings of an obscure clause, and illustrates the insatiable ambition from classical satire.
Reads the passage as the burden of Babylon and its king, finding the particular accomplishment in the night of the last king's feast.

positions.position: Nebuchadnezzar, proud and ambitious and inebriated with his successes.
Babylon's king, or the monarchy, or any proud oppressive power, with the particular accomplishment in Belshazzar.
Not the king only but the tyrannical empire with its people, a great company of robbers.
The Chaldaean, to whom the fundamental thought of the previous verse is now applied.
Not the Babylonian monarchs at all: reading it of the Chaldeans goes back to times before the first coming and breaks the thread of the prophecy.

outliers.claim: Quotes the satirist on Alexander, that one world did not suffice the youth of Pella, and adds the jest that the poet was right since at the last the sarcophagus proved too large for his body.
Hears the charge of drunkenness as a settled proverb, that it is a known fact wine is treacherous, and suspects the wisdom aphorism about wine the mocker stands behind it.

themes: Yea also, because he transgresseth by wine, he is a proud man, neither keepeth at home, who enlargeth his desire as hell, and is as death, and cannot be satisfied, but gathereth unto him all nations, and heapeth unto him all people:

6.pericope_label: Shall not all these take up a parable against him, and a taunting proverb against him, and say, Woe to him that increaseth that which is not his! how long? and to him that ladeth himself with thick clay! Shall they not rise up suddenly that shall bite thee, and awake that shall vex thee, and thou shalt be for booties unto them?

schools.summary: Lay out the five strophes of the taunt-song and press a commercial reading of the imagery, rejecting the received thick clay as a false etymology.
Refuse the usury sense on the ground that the answering words are biters and tormentors, and keep the taunt general or carry it forward past the Persians.
Supplies specimens of the proverbs and finds the fulfilment in the entry of the Persians through the diverted riverbed.

debates.question: Is the imagery of the taunt commercial or physical?

positions.position: Commercial throughout: he accumulates usury, the verb bite means to oppress with usury, and vex alludes to a creditor's forcible seizure.
Physical: the answering words are biters and tormentors, the verb means to bite and carries usury only in one conjugation, and the Septuagint gives biters.
Retains the older rendering of thick clay without arguing for it.
Reports the rendering thy usurers or thy creditors as what some give, without adopting it.
The Persians under Cyrus, entering through the bed of the diverted river.
The Christian emperors who overthrew the heathen ones and repaid the plundered with great gain.
Kept general: the common taunts of the many nations the empire had oppressed.

outliers.claim: Supplies specimen taunts of the kind meant: he who towered so high, behold how low he is fallen; he made himself a god, and behold he herds with the beasts of the field.
Sets out the architecture of the rest of the chapter as five woes in five strophes of three verses each, on rapacity, dynasty, building, the treatment of nations, and idolatry.

themes: Shall not all these take up a parable against him, and a taunting proverb against him, and say, Woe to him that increaseth that which is not his! how long? and to him that ladeth himself with thick clay!
Shall they not rise up suddenly that shall bite thee, and awake that shall vex thee, and thou shalt be for booties unto them?

8.pericope_label: Because thou hast spoiled many nations, all the remnant of the people shall spoil thee; because of men’s blood, and for the violence of the land, of the city, and of all that dwell therein. Woe to him that coveteth an evil covetousness to his house, that he may set his nest on high, that he may be delivered from the power of evil!

schools.summary: Read the violence as wreaked upon the land, and illustrate the nest set on high from the ancient measurements of Babylon's walls and towers.
Ground the sentence in retributive justice and warn that the riches meant to secure a house will ruin it.
Keeps the woe dynastic, the king aggrandising a family that was cut off with his son.

positions.position: The king aggrandising his family and seeking a permanent empire, both cut off with the death of his son.
Babylon stowing plunder in an impregnable treasure-house behind colossal walls.
The bishops of Rome, enriched by imperial donation and still not satisfied.

outliers.claim: Insists the taunts are not scurrilous jests but serious threatenings, and that in the common multitude who utter them we are to recognise the innumerable heralds of God's vengeance.
Identifies the remnant that spoils the spoiler with the survivors of the persecutions, who rose under Constantine and stripped the persecutors of power and wealth by just retaliation.

themes: Because thou hast spoiled many nations, all the remnant of the people shall spoil thee; because of men’s blood, and for the violence of the land, of the city, and of all that dwell therein.
Woe to him that coveteth an evil covetousness to his house, that he may set his nest on high, that he may be delivered from the power of evil!

10.pericope_label: Thou hast consulted shame to thy house by cutting off many people, and hast sinned against thy soul. For the stone shall cry out of the wall, and the beam out of the timber shall answer it.

schools.summary: State the charge in the terms of the text and make every stone reared by enforced labour an accuser.
Show the builder's glory turned to the disgrace he never intended, and admire the chorus of answering materials as a device against our dullness.
Explains the pairing of stone and beam from the ancient mode of walling and has the materials call out for vengeance.

debates.question: What does the crying stone mean?

positions.position: An architectural figure: courses of stone alternating with timber, the materials calling for vengeance because bought with spoil and lives.
Every stone in walls reared by the enforced labour of captives accuses the builder, and every spar attests the charge.
The stone cries to God for vengeance as if it had a voice, and the beam confirms the accusation.
Men within the corrupted body itself who cried out against it in sermons and writings, such as Bernard, Wycliffe and Huss.

outliers.claim: Notices that the materials are made to answer one another as in a chorus, in the way voices in lyric poetry take up the song by turns, and that the word rendered wood occurs nowhere else so that the versions have guessed at it.
Fixes the means by which the shame was consulted as the cutting off of many people, tying the clause to the dynastic ambition of the previous woe.

themes: Thou hast consulted shame to thy house by cutting off many people, and hast sinned against thy soul.
For the stone shall cry out of the wall, and the beam out of the timber shall answer it.

12.pericope_label: Woe to him that buildeth a town with blood, and stablisheth a city by iniquity! Behold, is it not of the Lord of hosts that the people shall labour in the very fire, and the people shall weary themselves for very vanity?

schools.summary: Gloss the means of the building as murder, transportation and tyranny, and show that the same preposition in both clauses makes the labour an equivalent in fire and in nothing.
Refuse to separate the blood from the iniquity, since plundering the helpless is killing by degrees, and explain the speaking stones as a remedy for our dullness.
Apply the woe to fortunes raised by the slave trade and read the ruin as a judgment for labour that receives nothing.

positions.position: The church of Rome, mystical Babylon, built by the blood of saints and established by exactions and indulgences.
The fortunes and buildings raised by the slave trade, whose walls seem composed of bones and cemented with blood.
Cities founded by the Chaldaean with the blood and property of subjugated strangers.

outliers.claim: Holds that the avaricious who do not kill outright yet suck men's blood and kill by degrees, since it is easier to undergo death at once than to pine away in want, so that wanton plundering is murder in the sight of God.

Observes that the same preposition governs both clauses and means an equivalent in, so the sense is to labour only for the fire and weary themselves all for nothing, as another prophet says of Babylon.

themes: Woe to him that buildeth a town with blood, and stablisheth a city by iniquity!
Behold, is it not of the Lord of hosts that the people shall labour in the very fire, and the people shall weary themselves for very vanity?

14.pericope_label: For the earth shall be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the Lord, as the waters cover the sea.

schools.summary: Corrects the preposition to as concerns the knowledge and sets the promise against the short-lived glory of Babylon, whose palaces were raised only for the fire.
Read the promise against the darkness of the exile, when God was hidden and the profane concluded there was no providence, and identify the glory that fills the earth as Christ's.
Offers three ascending applications, to Babylon, to the days of the Messiah, and to the universal spread of the gospel.

debates.question: What does the promise that the earth shall be filled refer to?

positions.position: Three things at once, in ascending order: the fall of Babylon, the preaching of the Messiah and his disciples, and the gospel over the whole globe.
The glory of Christ, both the essential glory of his person and the glory of his mediatorial office.
A contrast to Babylon's short-lived glory: what the nations built for the fire perishes, but this glory will not be effaced.
The judgment on Babylon, so remarkable that God's name would be celebrated through the whole world after a season in which he was hidden.

outliers.claim: States as a principle that the earth cannot perish until every continent, island and inhabitant has been illuminated with the light of the gospel.

Describes the sufferers as struck mute by their miseries, unable to bless God from the heart, while the profane concluded from the confusion that events fall out fortuitously and there is no divine providence.

themes: For the earth shall be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the Lord, as the waters cover the sea.

15.pericope_label: Woe unto him that giveth his neighbour drink, that puttest thy bottle to him, and makest him drunken also, that thou mayest look on their nakedness!

schools.summary: Take the drink figuratively, one refusing the literal story as groundless and the other applying the figure to methods used against Protestants after the Reformation.
Finds a historical culprit outside Babylon in the king who enticed the last kings of Judah into rebellion.
Reads the woe literally against the promoters of drunkenness and finds it verified in the king who forced his lords to pledge him.

debates.question: Is the giving of drink literal or figurative?

positions.position: Literal: an impeachment of the promoters of drunkenness, verified in the king who began the healths and compelled his company.
Metaphorical or allegorical throughout, and aimed at the whole empire rather than a king.
Figurative, of the alluring methods used to make Protestants forsake their religion after the Reformation.
A historical alliance: the Egyptian king who enticed the last kings of Judah into rebellion and left them exposed.

outliers.claim: Charges the Jewish interpreters with contriving fables whenever nothing certain occurs to them, and rejects the story of captive kings made drunk for sport on the ground that no history relates it.
Suggests that the later Persian law forbidding compulsion in drinking may have arisen from the example of the king who forced his thousand lords to pledge him.

themes: Woe unto him that giveth his neighbour drink, that puttest thy bottle to him, and makest him drunken also, that thou mayest look on their nakedness!

16.pericope_label: Thou art filled with shame for glory: drink thou also, and let thy foreskin be uncovered: the cup of the Lord’s right hand shall be turned unto thee, and shameful spewing shall be on thy glory. For the violence of Lebanon shall cover thee, and the spoil of beasts, which made them afraid, because of men’s blood, and for the violence of the land, of the city, and of all that dwell therein.

schools.summary: Mark where the last strophe begins, and read the violence of Lebanon as a raid on its cattle and a felling of its cedars for the palaces of Babylon.
Use the ground of the punishment to prove the drink was figurative, and find the shame worst in those who glory in it.
Explain the passed cup as exact retaliation and extend the violence to Judea and the city.

debates.question: What is the violence of Lebanon?

positions.position: Violence done to Lebanon: a raid on the cattle of its slopes and the felling of its cedars for Babylon's palaces, though some read it as a synecdoche for the Holy Land or the Temple.
Violence to men, cattle, Judea and the city, and possibly a threatening against Egypt rather than Chaldea.
The violence done to Judea, with the spoil of beasts as the havoc hunters make in destroying a whole kind.
Violence against the chosen people in particular, of which God is in a peculiar manner the avenger.

outliers.claim: Explains the cup from ancient table custom, all drinking from one vessel passed hand to hand, so that those who handed the nations the cup of idolatry receive back the cup of God's fury.

Finds the worst of the case in the absence of shame, the guilty counting it an honour to have brought others into uncleanness and glutting themselves on the sight instead of taking shame to themselves.

themes: Thou art filled with shame for glory: drink thou also, and let thy foreskin be uncovered: the cup of the Lord’s right hand shall be turned unto thee, and shameful spewing shall be on thy glory.
For the violence of Lebanon shall cover thee, and the spoil of beasts, which made them afraid, because of men’s blood, and for the violence of the land, of the city, and of all that dwell therein.

18.pericope_label: What profiteth the graven image that the maker thereof hath graven it; the molten image, and a teacher of lies, that the maker of his work trusteth therein, to make dumb idols?

schools.summary: Takes the teacher of lies to be the idol itself rather than a false prophet, and notes that the Hebrew pair rendered dumb nothings was chosen for its similarity of sound.
Explain why the true God must be named here, since a general belief in divine vengeance was common among the heathen and would leave the doctrine empty.
Directs the verse against idolatry in general and its princes and priests, and asks what any nation's idols ever did to save their worshippers.

debates.question: What is the derision aimed at?

positions.position: At the vain confidence of the Babylonian king, and the point of naming the God of Israel is that a bare belief in some heavenly justice was already common among the heathen.
At idolatry in general and every species of it, together with the princes, priests and people who practise and encourage it.
At the images whose worship the church of Rome enjoins, still in use after the Reformation.

outliers.claim: Identifies the teacher of lies with the idol itself, as pointing out false ways in opposition to God the teacher of truth, rather than with any false prophet.

Answers the prophet's question like an accountant: the images may profit the graver who is paid and the metal may fetch something if sold, but as deities they cannot hear a prayer or deliver from any distress.

themes: What profiteth the graven image that the maker thereof hath graven it; the molten image, and a teacher of lies, that the maker of his work trusteth therein, to make dumb idols?

19.pericope_label: Woe unto him that saith to the wood, Awake; to the dumb stone, Arise, it shall teach! Behold, it is laid over with gold and silver, and there is no breath at all in the midst of it. But the Lord is in his holy temple: let all the earth keep silence before him.

schools.summary: Render the woe plainly and locate the holy temple at Jerusalem, reading the verse as the turn from denunciation to the ode that follows.
Place the temple in heaven or in the church, and argue that the true God must be named after the idols are stripped away.
Contrast the breathless image with the meanest living brute, and take the commanded silence as reverence, submission and waiting.

positions.position: In heaven, the habitation of God's holiness, or else in the church, where he grants his presence to those who worship in spirit and truth.
At Jerusalem, where the true ruler of the world abides while the false worship prevails.
In the place of worship where there is no image at all and the oracles given are true and fulfilled in season.

outliers.claim: Judges superstition more tolerable than gross impiety, since the superstitious at least retain the principle that honour and worship are due to God, while the profane strive so far as they can to reduce him to nothing.
Charges the address to the wood in both its forms alike, the request that the image deliver and the request that it intercede, since to address a block as one addresses God is detestable either way.

themes: Woe unto him that saith to the wood, Awake; to the dumb stone, Arise, it shall teach! Behold, it is laid over with gold and silver, and there is no breath at all in the midst of it.
But the Lord is in his holy temple: let all the earth keep silence before him.
